query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporate a minor addition of yttrium (Y) to leverage reactive element effects for improved oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with established mechanical performance but poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Alloy a small amount (e.g., 0.5–1 at.%) of yttrium into the base composition.
generation.conditions: Service at high temperatures (around 1000 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere (air) with mechanical loading conditions similar to the original testing (strain rates 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹) and exposure times ranging from tens to hundreds of hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of finely dispersed Y₂O₃ particles at the oxide/alloy interface or within the protective surface scale.
generation.mechanism: Yttrium segregates to the oxide grain boundaries during oxidation, enhancing oxide scale adhesion and reducing its growth rate. This reactive element effect is known to improve oxidation resistance in high-temperature alloys while maintaining the core microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: A slower oxidation rate and a more adherent, stable oxide scale form on the alloy surface, leading to improved oxygen resistance without compromising its tensile ductility and yield strength.
generation.baseline: The untreated cast alloy suffers from rapid oxygen ingress and embrittlement at 1000 °C in air.
generation.boundary: The Y addition must be limited (0.5–1 at.%) to ensure it does not significantly alter the alloy’s primary phase structure or mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: Moderate; while reactive element effects are well documented in other high-temperature alloys, the optimal Y content and its distribution in this HEA need to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy batches: one with a 0.5–1 at.% Y addition and one without. Expose both to high-temperature oxidation (1000 °C in air) for a predetermined period (e.g., 100 hours) and compare their oxidation behavior and mechanical properties.
measurements: Use TEM/SEM to inspect oxide scale morphology and Y₂O₃ dispersion.
Conduct tensile tests at 1000 °C to evaluate yield strength and ductility.
Monitor oxidation kinetics through thermogravimetric analysis.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped alloy does not show a measurable improvement in oxidation resistance or if its mechanical properties at high temperature are compromised relative to the undoped sample, then the hypothesis is refuted.

In 2004, Professor Yeh and his group published the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) []. He defined high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as having five or more major elements beneath 5–35 at.%, and minor elements below five at.%. In 2006, he also established four core effects of HEAs []: High-entropy, severe-lattices-distortion, sluggish-diffusion, and the cocktail effect. With the new concepts, scientists are able to develop and expand alloys without restrictions [,,,,]. Some HEAs have been found to have attractive properties on diffusion [], oxidation [], corrosion [], fatigue [], creep [], fracture toughness [], and elevated-temperature strength []. High-entropy superalloys (HESAs) [], eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [], light-weight HEAs (LWHEAs) [], refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], etc. have been proposed and attract increased attention.
